To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the U.K. system of hospital finance and performance evaluation has an inherent internal inconsistency, while the DRG system has an implicit performance evaluation system which is not necessarily related to the characteristics of patients served by the hospital.

the U.K. system of hospital funding and appraisal is inconsistent, and that the U.S. DRG system of hospital funding is a form of performance appraisal that is not necessarily consistent with the objectives of the system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the incentive structure of the U.K. system on the allocation of resources between the sectors of the system and the implications for the health status of the population.
the impact of the U.S. and U.K. approaches to cost containment on the performance of hospital systems and the implications for health status of the population.
the implications of the U.K. policy of cost containment on the quality of health services.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the U.K. system is better than the U.S. system in that it is more likely to achieve the objective of providing a comprehensive health care system for all, and that it has the potential to be better than the U.K. in that the U.S. has developed a system for the appraisal of hospital services which is more sensitive to the needs of the patient.
the U.K. policy is a more effective method of controlling the cost of the hospital sector, but that the U.S. policy is a superior method of controlling the overall cost of the health care sector.
the U.K. policy of imposing cash limits on the hospital system is more successful in controlling the resource costs of the system than the U.S. policy of funding hospital services on a DRG system.

we are all working in a hospital system which is under-funded, and which is therefore under-performing.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the incentives generated by the U.K. cash limits and the U.S.DRGs are similar and have similar effects on the health care system.
the U.S. policy of using a DRG based funding system to control hospital costs is not a panacea for the control of hospital costs in the U.K.; it is a different way of achieving the same end.

the incentives generated by the U.K. policy for the hospital system, in the form of the imposition of cash-limits and performance appraisal, are similar to those generated by the U.S. policy in the form of DRG based funding.
